newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi expands gold mine after new discovery.
newsitem.headline: Saudi expands gold mine after new discovery.

text.p: A new discovery of high-yielding gold ore at Saudi Arabia's largest gold mine has prompted an overhaul of the mill and increased the mine's expected life by about four years, a Saudi official said on Wednesday.

Speaking by telephone from Riyadh, the official told Reuters that Mahd adh Dhahab, about 280 km northeast of the Red Sea port of Jeddah, was being overhauled to raise throughput capacity by a third and keep the mine in the gold business until at least the year 2006 from a previous forecast 2002 close.

"We are trying to increase the capacity of the mill. We have discovered additional ore reserves and we are doing some modification and upgrading," he said, adding that the work was expected to be completed by April.

The mine -- in the Arabian Shield, which stretches along the kingdom's Red Sea coast -- produced 157,000 ounces of the metal last year, down from 1995's 169,000 ounces. The drop was attributed to shutdowns needed for equipment overhaul.
The world's largest oil producer and exporter has two gold mines, the other is Sukhaybarat which produced 2.60 tonnes last year, and has plans to develop another four.
Although not a competitor with gold heavyweights like South Africa, which produces about 500 tonnes a year, Saudi Arabia does have some high-yielding ore not far from the surface.
Operating costs are lower, but officials say as most mineral deposits are in remote parts of the vast desert kingdom, infrastructure development is expensive.

"The overhaul will increase throughput of gold ore by 30-35 percent, but the increase in gold output will not be by as much because the yield of the new discovery is slightly lower than the average grade of the original reserve," the official said.
"This year we expect over 170,000 ounces and next year something like 185,000 ounces from Mahd adh Dhahab," he added.

The mine, in an area of rocky outcrops and low hills rising from a plateau of stony desert, also produced about 479,000 ounces of silver and 900 tonnes of copper in 1996. It plans to start production of zinc concentrate this year.

State-owned Mahd adh Dhahab, which means cradle of gold and was first mined about 3,000 years ago, resumed gold production in 1988. At that time, the reserve was estimated at around 1.2 million tonnes with an average yield of 26 grammes per tonne.

"So far we have processed over 1.5 million tonnes at 26.5 grammes per tonne. So we have exceeded what the feasibility study foresaw. But we still have two million tonnes to go at 24-25 grammes per tonne," he added, referring to the new find.
"We still expect to find more ore reserves, but we have not done all the drilling yet," the official said.
This would mean that the mine, whose gold reserves were initially expected to be depleted before the turn of the century, would be exploited for another eight to 10 years.
